description: In 1953, Watson and Crick described the DNA double helix. Behind this glory, the crucial work of Rosalind Franklin.

hero.hook: The shape of a molecule… and the secret of heredity.

blocks.text: We knew that traits pass from parents to children. But what chemical object carries this information? In the middle of the 20th century, the answer became clearer: **DNA**.
In **1953**, **James Watson** and **Francis Crick** published a famous model: the **double propeller**. This form explains how DNA can copy itself.
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a long molecule found in our cells. It contains chemical “letters” that form a code. But in the 1940s and 1950s, we did not yet know its 3D form.
Without the form, it is difficult to understand how this code can duplicate itself with each cell division.

blocks.caption: Photo 51 of Rosalind Franklin reveals a helical structure.

blocks.text: **Rosalind Franklin**, physicist and chemist, obtains X-ray images of DNA. Her famous **Picture 51** shows clear evidence of a helix.
Watson and Crick see this data (under conditions now considered unfair to Franklin) and build their model. Franklin died in 1958; the 1962 Nobel will go to Watson, Crick and Wilkins, not her.
Franklin also did major work on viruses. Its role in DNA has long been underestimated in popular accounts.

blocks.caption: Two complementary strands: the copy becomes imaginable.

blocks.text: Two strands wrap around each other. The letters face each other in pairs. When the strands separate, each can serve as a model to reconstruct the other. Heredity becomes an understandable chemical mechanism.
From this discovery are born modern genetics, sequencing, DNA tests, gene therapies. And also ethical debates: what to do with this power?
In **1953**, the double helix model explains how DNA stores and copies information from living things. Franklin provided decisive evidence too long erased from the narrative.

subject: sciences
title: The structure of DNA
